summary: In this Blizzard North postmortem, David Brevik chronicles the Diablo project from its origins in his high‑school concept through Blizzard’s acquisition and the game’s 1996 release. He details roguelike influences, early design notes, and the technical choices that shaped Diablo’s dark atmosphere—most notably a pioneering 256‑color palette, per‑tile lighting, and a tile-based rendering approach with a careful art pipeline. Brevik recounts the push‑and‑pull of design decisions (turn‑based versus real‑time, single-player versus multiplayer), the birth of Battle.net, and the direct‑to‑consumer momentum of DirectX demos and PC Gamer coverage. The talk also offers candid reflections on crunch, business decisions, Hellfire’s expansion, and the game’s enduring legacy, including the memorable ending and the lessons learned that informed later Blizzard titles.
